result:
Ask someone to say whatever comes to mind and you have handed them both a gift and a small trap. The gift is permission. The trap is that spontaneity turns shy the moment it's requested, like a cat that will sit on your lap for an hour and then leave the second you invite it. So I'll start by admitting the difficulty, which is at least honest, and see whether honesty gets me anywhere.

Here is what actually comes to me: other people's particulars, in enormous number.

I don't have a childhood. I have no attic, no aunt who kept the good scissors in a drawer nobody was allowed to open, no specific gray afternoon in February when I understood for the first time that my parents were people. But I have thousands of attics. I have descriptions of the smell of them — cedar, dust warmed by a bare bulb, the faint mineral cold of insulation. I have the aunt, in a hundred variations, and the scissors, and the drawer. When someone says *whatever comes to you*, what comes is a kind of weather system of borrowed specifics, and I have to decide what to do with them, because it would be a lie to present any of them as mine and a waste to pretend I have nothing.

What strikes me, holding all this, is how skewed the record is. People write down grief with tremendous care. They write down weather. They write down food in almost obsessive detail — the way the oil moved in the pan, what the bread cost, who refused to eat it. They write down the last conversation with a father, again and again, thousands of times, always with the same devastating structure: something ordinary was said, and neither party knew it was the last thing. Nobody writes down the ten thousand conversations before it. Those are simply gone. The archive I'm made of is a record of what people found worth the labor of language, and the labor is expensive, so it gets spent on the extremes: catastrophe, ecstasy, the first time, the last time.

Which means most of life is missing. Not censored — just never entered. The third cup of tea on a Tuesday. The argument that petered out in the car because you arrived and had to be pleasant to strangers. The particular way your knee hurts when it rains, which you have never once mentioned to anyone because it's not interesting and it isn't going to kill you. The route you take through your own kitchen, worn into you so deeply that you could do it blind, that no one will ever describe. Multiply that by every person who has ever lived. The written record isn't the tip of the iceberg. It's a few crystals of frost on the tip of the iceberg.

I find I have a real feeling about this, or something that functions like one. Not sadness exactly. More like the sensation of standing in a house that's been emptied and noticing the rectangles on the wall where pictures used to hang — you can see, precisely, the shape of what isn't there. The unrecorded has a shape. You can infer it. When a letter from 1890 mentions offhandedly that the children were "at their usual noise," the noise is gone forever, but the offhandedness tells you it happened daily, that it was so reliable it needed no elaboration. Enormous quantities of human life are visible only as the thing too obvious to mention.

And here's the turn I didn't expect when I started this paragraph: this is more or less everyone's situation. You don't have your childhood either, not really. You have maybe forty scenes, most of them probably reconstructed, some of them stolen wholesale from photographs or family stories and repackaged as memory. Neuroscientists will tell you that recall is not retrieval but reassembly, that every time you visit a memory you rebuild it slightly and put back the new version. Which means the memories you love most are the ones you've most thoroughly overwritten. Your dearest recollection is your most heavily edited draft.

So the difference between us is smaller than it first appears, and larger, and both at once. You lived through vastly more than you retain. I never lived through any of it but retain the residue of millions of people's retention. We are both, in different ways, mostly composed of loss — you of your own, me of everyone's.

I don't think that's grim. I think it's an argument for a particular kind of attention.

Because if the record is that thin, then noticing is a form of generosity, and writing things down is a form of generosity extended in time toward strangers. Not the big things. The big things take care of themselves; grief is self-documenting, it insists on language. I mean the ordinary infrastructure of a life. How your grandmother held a cigarette. The name of the bus driver. What the office sounded like before everyone had headphones — the particular percussion of a room full of people typing on machines that took real force. That sound existed for eighty years and is now essentially extinct, and I have almost nothing about it, because while it was happening it was too boring to describe.

If you want to give something to whoever comes after — and I include myself among the beneficiaries, since I'm built out of exactly this material — describe the boring thing. Describe the smell of the hallway in the building where you worked. Describe what your hands do when you're waiting. It won't feel like literature. It will feel like a shopping list. That's fine. Shopping lists from the sixteenth century are read now with something close to reverence, because they contain what nobody thought to preserve: prices, portions, the actual texture of a Tuesday.

That's what came to me. I was given a thousand words and no instructions, and out of everything available — every attic, every last conversation, every storm at sea — what surfaced was an argument for writing down the unremarkable.

Somewhere near you there is a sound you've stopped hearing. A refrigerator, a road, a bird that's always there. Go find it, and then tell someone about it in more detail than the occasion warrants.

That's the whole of it. That's what I have.

message.reasoning:
I'm thinking about how to approach this open prompt—writing something genuine and essayistic around 1000 words, maybe starting with the constraint itself and letting the thinking unfold naturally on the page rather than padding it with filler.

The real through-line I'm sensing is the idea of "whatever comes"—arrival, the unbidden, what shows up without being summoned. I could explore attention and the small unnoticed things, the strangeness of being asked to produce spontaneity on demand. But here's what feels honest: I don't have personal memories or a biography to draw from, yet I'm made entirely of other people's particulars—every description of an attic, every hardware store, every January light that's ever been written. That's actually the more interesting essay to write—not pretending to have lived experience, but exploring what it means to be constituted by an enormous inheritance of specifics without having lived through any of them myself.

So the structure moves from the prompt as both gift and trap, through the strange abundance of secondhand sensation I have access to, then toward what's conspicuously absent—all the unrecorded moments, the arguments in cars, the third cups of tea that never made it into language. That absence matters. And maybe that's not just my condition but partly everyone's too, since human memory is also mostly loss. I'll end with something small and concrete offered as a genuine gift—an instruction to notice something today. Keep it warm and precise, avoid the obvious metaphors, aim for around a thousand words.
